items.headline: ANSWERED: Brent did NOT round-trip — it held $83.55 and broke out to ~$86.5 (+3.5%), a 4th straight up session
items.summary: The level we told him to watch. Front-month Brent traded $86.50 intraday (+$2.95, +3.53%) and WTI $80.98 (+$2.80, +3.58%), both reconciled against Friday's $83.55 and $78.18 settles. There was never a meaningful break back below. IMPORTANT CURVE NUANCE: the move was NOT prompt-led — deferred contracts rallied harder (Nov +3.82%, Dec +3.88%, Jan-27 +3.83% vs Oct +3.53%), so the Oct-Nov spread narrowed from ~1.90 to 1.69 and Oct-Dec from 3.56 to 3.39. The curve stayed backwardated but FLATTENED, meaning the bid was in deferred barrels rather than prompt scarcity — more a repricing of the whole strip than an acute supply squeeze. These are INTRADAY futures, not settles; the US session is still open.
items.actionable: The Gulf premium is sticking rather than fading, which is the opposite of the last several geopolitical spikes — so Sunday's thesis was right on direction and Monday's early fade was the head-fake, not the signal. But read the flat curve honestly: this is the market repricing the whole strip, not panicking about prompt barrels. The second-order effect is the one that matters to you — crude +3.5% is reviving the inflation impulse that Friday's payrolls had just dismantled.

items.headline: 10Y yield climbs to a month high at 4.70% as oil revives inflation worry; September hike odds ~46%, down from ~64% a week ago
items.summary: The US 10-year yield rose to 4.68% Monday — its highest level so far this month — explicitly attributed to rising oil prices adding to inflation concerns, itself tied to 'growing uncertainty over a deal between the US and Iran to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.' The same page's data header showed 4.70%, +0.044 on the day; a separate mid-morning read had 4.684%, +0.028. Both imply the same prior close of ~4.656%, so the move is about +4.4bp and I quote the 4.68-4.70% band rather than a single figure. The 30-year is 5.24% on the same page, roughly +4bp against the 5.20% Friday reference — the long end is selling off in step, not lagging. Fed pricing: September hike odds now around 46%, no-change about 54%. Note the direction the source actually supports is DOWN over the week, from roughly 64% a week ago, driven by Friday's payrolls contraction; I have no verified intraday Friday low, so I make no claim that odds have 'firmed back' within the last session.
items.actionable: This is the cross-current. Oil at +3.5% has pushed the 10Y to a one-month high of 4.70%, rebuilding the September hike case that the payrolls contraction had dismantled three sessions ago. Your S-REITs and developers — which get their first mark tomorrow after the SGX holiday — face a higher discount rate than when they last traded.

items.headline: Silver hits a seven-week high at ~$65.1 spot (+2.5%) — the largest position in the book is working hard
items.summary: Spot silver traded $65.11 per troy ounce, +$1.57 (+2.47%), an implied previous close of exactly $63.54 matching Friday's published spot close, so the percent change is verified. That is silver's highest level in seven weeks (the source's own summary text still references a seven-week high at 'over $63.50', lagging the current quote). Drivers cited: repricing of Fed hike expectations after July's payrolls contraction lowering the holding cost of non-yielding assets, plus industrial demand — Chinese imports of silver-bearing ores surged 62.5% year-on-year in June to 219,000 tonnes on solar and grid buildout. CORRECTION TO A FIGURE THAT CIRCULATED EARLIER: gold is NOT $4,406-4,417. Gold is $4,361.34, +$17.91 (+0.41%), against Friday's $4,343.43 spot close — a firm but unremarkable day, roughly a quarter of the move the higher figure implied. These are INTRADAY/spot levels, not settles.
items.actionable: Silver has run from ~$55.6 in late July to ~$65.1 — roughly +17%, and at 1.6x leverage that is a substantial gain on the IBKR equity. It is now rallying on the oil-driven inflation impulse, which is a different engine from last week's dovish-Fed rally. Note the tension: the same impulse that is lifting silver could revive the September hike that would hurt it.

items.headline: DIVERGENCE: GDX -0.14% while gold +0.41% near a two-month high and SILJ runs +2.09% — gold miners not confirming
items.summary: GDX INTRADAY $89.76 at 12:18 PM ET, change -$0.13 = -0.14%, previous close $89.89 (Friday 7 Aug close), volume 10,643,695 shares [finviz.com/quote.ashx?t=GDX]. So gold miners are marginally RED on a day gold spot is +0.41% ($4,361.34/oz, +$17.91) and sits near its highest in two months — TradingEconomics' text reads 'near the highest in two months,' not a fresh two-month high, so the metal is approaching the level rather than printing it [tradingeconomics.com/commodity/gold]. By contrast SILJ (junior silver miners) INTRADAY $29.75 at 12:18 PM ET, +$0.61 = +2.09%, previous close $29.14, volume 3,010,335 [finviz.com/quote.ashx?t=SILJ] — tracking silver's move closely. SILJ's one-week performance is +19.81% and one-month +16.99%, though it remains -6.30% on the quarter and -9.22% over six months, and sits well below its $41.10 52-week high against a $16.16 low. Both are INTRADAY levels, US session in progress. The split is clean and sector-specific: it is a gold-miner phenomenon, not a mining-equity phenomenon, since the silver miners are performing exactly as the metal would imply.
items.actionable: Worth watching closely: the gold miners are NOT following gold today (GDX -0.14% against gold +0.41%) while the silver miners are (SILJ +2.09%). After GDX's 20%+ week that is either healthy consolidation or the first sign the miner rally has run ahead of the metal. Do not assume the sleeve moves as one.

items.headline: Hang Seng closed 25,937.49 (+1.05%); Hang Seng Tech 4,919 (+1.3%) — final closes
items.summary: FINAL CLOSE, Asia session complete. Hang Seng Index finished at 25,937.49, up 269.46 points or +1.05%, on turnover of HK$240.28bn. Hang Seng Tech Index closed 4,919, up 61 points or +1.3%. I verified the index level against Friday's confirmed 25,668.03 close: 25,668.03 + 269.46 = 25,937.49, and 269.46/25,668.03 = 1.0498%, so both level and change are correct as stated. This matters because TradingEconomics was simultaneously publishing the level as 26,010 with the same (correct) +269.46 change — a ~73-point error I rejected. Breadth leadership came from consumer, property and precious-metals names; chipmakers and AI stocks fell. Guotai Junan International was in focus ahead of a trading resumption following its parent's HK$28.6bn privatisation proposal.
items.actionable: A clean +1.05% close on healthy HK$240bn turnover — but the gain came from consumer, property and precious-metals names, NOT tech. Do not read Hang Seng Tech +1.3% as broad tech strength; chips were negative underneath it.

items.headline: HK tech split on soft China CPI/PPI: Xiaomi +2.07%, Tencent +0.54%, SMIC -1.05% — all final closes
items.summary: FINAL CLOSES for all three of his HK tech holdings. Xiaomi (1810.HK) closed HK$27.62 vs HK$27.06 Friday, +HK$0.56 or +2.07% — I computed this myself from the two closes and it matches the published figure. Tencent (0700.HK) closed HK$481.40 vs HK$478.80, +HK$2.60 or +0.54% — also recomputed and matched. SMIC (0981.HK) closed HK$66.20 vs HK$66.90, -HK$0.70 or -1.05%, giving back part of Friday's +2.37%. So the response to China's undershooting July CPI (+0.5%, a six-month low) and PPI (+3.5%) was not a uniform tech bid: the platform and hardware names took the softer-inflation/easier-policy read positively, while the semiconductor name went the other way in sympathy with the region-wide AI/memory de-rating. On his 26,662 Xiaomi units the day's move is worth approximately +HK$14,931 (my arithmetic: 26,662 x HK$0.56). Earlier vendor snapshots circulating for these names (Tencent +0.7%, Xiaomi +0.4%) were intraday prints, not closes, and disagree with the verified closing data — I used the settled figures.
items.actionable: Xiaomi did the heavy lifting: +2.07% is worth roughly +HK$14,900 on your 26,662 units. It behaved like a consumer stock, which is exactly where the money rotated. SMIC (-1.05%) is the name exposed to the AI/memory de-rating spreading through Asian semis — that is the one to watch, not Tencent, which is trading defensively into Wednesday's results.

items.headline: Mainland closed higher but rotated hard out of AI and chips into precious metals — Shanghai 3,966.59 (+0.67%)
items.summary: FINAL CLOSES. Shanghai Composite 3,966.59, up 26.55 points or +0.67%, verified against Friday's confirmed 3,940.04 close (26.55/3,940.04 = 0.674%). Shenzhen Component 14,316, up 5 points or +0.04% — essentially unchanged, and effectively flat despite the Shanghai gain, which itself tells you the growth-heavy board was capped. Turnover was heavy: roughly RMB1.17trn in Shanghai and RMB1.36trn in Shenzhen. The sector split was the story and it was violent for a day the index closed up: the CSI 300 Telecommunication Services Index fell 3.5%, the CSI AI Index fell 3%, and the Cloud Computing Index lost 2%, while poultry, dairy and precious-metals sectors led gains. Note the Shenzhen figure is single-sourced to RTHK; I flag that, though RTHK's other two index figures (HSI 25,937 and Shanghai 3,966) both reconciled exactly against independently verified closes, which gives reasonable confidence in the third.
items.actionable: The cleanest read of the day. With CPI at +0.5% and PPI +3.5% both undershooting, mainland money did NOT buy reflation — it bought defensives and precious-metals miners and sold AI (CSI AI Index -3%, Telecom -3.5%, Cloud -2%) on RMB2.5trn of combined turnover. That rotation supports your miners and works against the chip end of your HK exposure.

items.headline: Korea's index stabilised (+0.65%) but the memory complex did not — SK Hynix -0.14%, Samsung -0.43%; Nikkei +2.08%
items.summary: FINAL CLOSES (Asia, Monday 10 Aug). Nikkei 225 closed 66,970.22, up 1,363.51 points or +2.08%, led by AI and chip-linked names after Wall Street's Friday rally and the weak US payrolls print. KOSPI closed 6,299.66, up 40.89 points or +0.65% — verified against Friday's confirmed 6,258.77 close (40.89/6,258.77 = 0.653%), which matches the published figure exactly. So the KOSPI index stabilised after last week's crash. But the memory names did not: SK Hynix closed 1,420,000 won, DOWN 0.14%, and Samsung Electronics closed 230,000 won, DOWN 0.43%. Both were negative on an up day — the index bounce came from elsewhere in the market. Per separate reporting (Aju Press, Seoul Economic Daily), SK Hynix had fallen 4.88% on Friday on reports Nvidia may use less HBM than originally planned in Rubin Ultra, its next-generation AI chip, a concern to which SK Hynix has more exposure than Samsung; the KOSPI fell 4.58% Thursday and a further 0.60% Friday. That thesis was not refuted Monday; the stock simply stopped falling. SoftBank Group closed 5,484 yen (-1.22%), Kioxia 48,010 yen (+0.59%).
items.actionable: The index stabilised but the memory complex did not — SK Hynix and Samsung both closed NEGATIVE on an up day. The AI/memory unwind has not finished, which is the read-across risk for SMIC.

items.headline: CPI setup for Wednesday: Cleveland Fed nowcast points to a soft +0.09% headline but a stickier +0.21% core
items.summary: July CPI lands Wednesday 12 August. The Cleveland Fed nowcast, as of 6 August, looks for headline CPI +0.09% month-on-month and 3.42% year-on-year, with core CPI +0.21% month-on-month and 2.52% year-on-year. The same nowcast already carries an August headline estimate of +0.38% m/m — a sharp acceleration — which is where the current oil move would start showing up. PPI follows later in the week. IMPORTANT CAVEAT ON A FIGURE YOU MAY SEE ELSEWHERE: the article carrying this nowcast was published 10 August but quotes CME FedWatch September odds of 'nearly 55% hike / 45% hold' explicitly as of 6 August — that is a PRE-payrolls number and is stale by four days. The live figure is ~46% hike / ~54% hold. Do not let the 55% into the dashboard.
items.actionable: Wednesday remains the week: CPI and Tencent results the same day. A soft headline with a sticky core is the awkward outcome — it would not clearly resolve the September hike either way, leaving both your metals and your REITs in limbo.

items.headline: Hormuz still shut: Araghchi demands blockade lifted plus compensation; Iran-Oman close but not done
items.summary: The Monday developments that explain the oil bid. Per TradingEconomics' Brent commentary, Iranian FM Abbas Araghchi said Tehran is NOT currently holding direct talks with the US and reiterated that reopening Hormuz would require Washington to lift its blockade of Iranian shipping and provide compensation for damages; the same page carries President Trump saying Washington was now 'low-keying it' [tradingeconomics.com/commodity/brent-crude-oil]. Al Jazeera frames the same conditions as Washington easing sanctions and providing war reparations, and notes Iran has repeatedly insisted on the right to control shipping in the strait, which cuts against freedom-of-navigation norms. Al Jazeera reports Iran and Oman were 'close to an agreement' on Hormuz, but the waterway will not reopen until those conditions are met — framework close, reopening not. The UAE on Saturday condemned what it said was an Iranian missile attack on a vessel owned by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company. Hard number on the disruption: only 8 to 15 vessels crossed the strait between 4 and 6 August, against roughly 130 transits before the conflict began in late February. The International Maritime Organization counts at least 64 violent incidents and 17 deaths involving commercial vessels since the war began, most blamed on Iran. Al Jazeera's own price stamp is October Brent at $84.11 at 07:30 GMT, up 0.7% — an early reading, superseded by the $86.53 level later in the session.
items.actionable: Araghchi is demanding the blockade lifted plus compensation; the Iran-Oman lane deal is close but not done and does not itself reopen the strait. This is why the premium is sticking rather than fading.

items.headline: MP Materials +7.2% intraday on no fresh headline; GDX/SILJ Monday levels unverified — anchor to Friday's real closes
items.summary:
MP Materials traded up 7.2% intraday Monday 10 August (INTRADAY — the US session has not closed; source published ~11:02 ET). Per the source, no single new headline drove it; the move is attributed to continued reaction to the 6 August Q2 print plus the magnet ramp, Texas expansion and defence demand theme. Q2 figures (separately sourced, not in the cited article): revenue $108.49M, a 9.35% beat of the Zacks consensus; NdPr production +41% YoY to 840 metric tons and NdPr sales volume +127% YoY to 1,006 metric tons — sales more than doubled, production did not. Consolidated revenue plus PPA income was $126.1M, more than double a year earlier.

On Energy Fuels (UUUU), the confirmed items are from 5-6 August, not Monday: Q2-2026 results released 5 August with revenue of $25.11M against a $30.2M Zacks consensus, a 16.9% miss, and a net loss of $33.4M ($0.13/sh) driven largely by ASM/VAC transaction costs; Roth/MKM then upgraded UUUU to Buy from Neutral on valuation with an unchanged $16 target. No verified Monday move for UUUU.

MINERS — MONDAY IS UNKNOWN, NOT FLAT. I could not obtain a trustworthy live Monday quote for GDX or SILJ, so nothing Monday-dated is reported for either. The Friday 7 August closes, verified against exchange history, are GDX $89.89 (+7.11% on the day, prior close $83.92) and GDXJ $117.62 (+7.51%), capping the miners' best week in over a year at roughly +21% and +23% respectively over five sessions. Note that widely circulated figures of GDX $89.73 and GDXJ $116.78 are pre-close intraday prints from a wire story filed before the bell — do not use them as closes. Separately, if the dashboard is carrying GDX near $83.68, that is a correct but stale 5 August close, not a corrupt quote; it simply needs refreshing to Friday's $89.89. With silver spot +2.47% and gold firmer Monday, the miners are very likely up again, but that must be confirmed from a live feed before it enters the P&L.
items.actionable: A 7.2% intraday move on no fresh headline, consistent with the broad precious/strategic-metals bid. GDX and SILJ Monday levels are anchored to verified sources rather than this print.

items.headline: DATA INTEGRITY: two bad prints rejected — a Brent quote off a stale reference, and a Hang Seng level 73 points wrong
items.summary: A Fortune Brent print of $87.55 was rejected because its reference price was a prior morning's level rather than Friday's settle. Separately, TradingEconomics was publishing the Hang Seng level as 26,010 while carrying the correct +269.46 change — a ~73-point error; the verified close is 25,937.49, which reconciles exactly to Friday's 25,668.03. Vendor intraday snapshots for Tencent (+0.7%) and Xiaomi (+0.4%) were also discarded in favour of settled closes.
items.actionable: Third consecutive day a bad vendor figure was caught before publication. The rule introduced yesterday — only trust a percent-change when its implied previous close reconciles to the known settle — is now doing real work.
